maml:description.maml:para: Runs a live traceroute with per-hop packet-loss and latency statistics, in the style of the Linux mtr tool.

Start-Mtr traces the network path to a target and continuously re-probes every hop, maintaining running statistics for each one: packet loss percentage, probes sent, and the last, average, best, worst, and standard deviation of the round-trip times. The table redraws in place once per cycle. Press Ctrl+C to stop.

The header line shows the target address, the local source address probes are sent from, and the name and IPv4 index of the interface that owns it. Without -Interface this is the address the operating system's routing table selects; with -Interface the header appends [bound] to indicate probes are explicitly source-bound. In TCP mode the header also shows the port and, once the target answers, whether it is open or closed.

The path is discovered incrementally, as mtr does: the trace begins at hop 1 and extends one hop per cycle, so only hops that have actually been probed appear. The search stops when the destination answers, when a router reports the destination unreachable, or after five consecutive hops return nothing - five silent routers in a row means the path is dead or filtered from that point, and probing further adds no information.

On Windows the trace is implemented directly against the ICMP API and requires no elevation. Probes run several at a time rather than strictly sequentially, which makes it substantially faster than tracert, which probes one hop at a time with a four-second timeout per probe. Concurrency is deliberately bounded: probing every TTL at once causes the Windows ICMP path to serialise the sends, which inflates every measured time and makes responsive hops appear lost.

On Linux and macOS, Start-Mtr delegates to the installed mtr binary and passes through the equivalent options. This is deliberate: .NET's Ping class falls back to invoking /bin/ping when unprivileged, and that path does not reliably expose the intermediate hop address from a TTL-expired reply, which is the one thing a traceroute depends on. If the mtr binary is not installed, Start-Mtr reports an error explaining how to install it.
The hostname or IPv4 address to trace to. Hostnames are resolved to their first IPv4 address before the trace begins. IPv6 targets are not supported.

command:parameter.maml:name: TcpPort

maml:description.maml:para: Trace using TTL-limited TCP connections to this port instead of ICMP echo, equivalent to mtr's -T -P options. Use this when ICMP is filtered along the path, or to find where traffic to one specific service is being blocked - a firewall may drop TCP 445 while passing ICMP straight through, so the two traces can end at different hops.

Windows only. A TCP socket cannot see the ICMP Time Exceeded messages routers send back, so hop identities are recovered by capturing them with Npcap, through the companion MtrCapture.dll that sits alongside MtrCheck.dll in the module's Bin folder. If Npcap is not installed, MtrCapture.dll is missing, or the Npcap driver was installed with access restricted to Administrators, Start-Mtr issues a warning and continues with every intermediate hop shown as ??? - the destination is still identified, so the trace still reports how far away the target is and whether the port answers.
A target that answers with RST counts as reached: the host is there, the port simply is not listening. The header distinguishes this by showing "closed (RST)" rather than "open".

command:parameter.dev:defaultValue: None - ICMP echo is used when this is not specified

maml:description.maml:para: Skip reverse-DNS lookups and display IP addresses only. Equivalent to mtr's -n option. Without this switch, hostnames are resolved on background threads and appear in the table a cycle or two after the address itself, so a slow resolver never stalls the live display.

command:parameter.maml:name: Interface

maml:description.maml:para: Send probes from a specific network interface, rather than letting the routing table choose. Equivalent to mtr's -I option. Accepts the interface friendly name, its description, or its ID; use Get-NetAdapter to list the available names on Windows.

In ICMP mode this uses IcmpSendEcho2Ex, which accepts an explicit source address and does not require Administrator privileges. In TCP mode the probe socket is simply bound to that address. If the named interface has no IPv4 address, Start-Mtr reports an error listing the interfaces that do.

command:parameter.dev:defaultValue: The interface chosen by the routing table

maml:description.maml:para: The maximum number of hops to probe, from 1 to 255. Note that the trace usually stops well before this: reaching the destination, an unreachable report, or five consecutive silent hops all end the search. Raising this value will not reveal hops beyond a run of five silent ones.

Seconds to wait between cycles, from 1 to 60, once the path has been discovered. While the trace is still extending to new hops it cycles faster than this, so a long path appears in a second or two rather than taking one second per hop.
How long to wait for each individual probe, in milliseconds, from 100 to 10000. Probes that do not answer within this window count as lost for that hop.

Worth raising in TCP mode. A TCP SYN retransmits when a reply is slow, so a probe with a perfectly adequate TTL can still exceed the default 1000 ms and be recorded as a failure, which places the destination a hop or two further out than it really is.
Start-Mtr does not accept pipeline input.
Start-Mtr writes its table directly to the host and returns nothing to the pipeline. It is an interactive display tool rather than a source of data for scripts.

maml:alert.maml:para: A hop's loss figure describes only that router's willingness to answer about itself. It says nothing about traffic passing through it. Generating an ICMP Time Exceeded message is control-plane work that routers rate-limit aggressively or disable outright, while forwarding continues untouched - it is common for a gateway to show 90 percent or more here yet answer every ping normally.

The rule for telling artifact from fault: every packet reaching a later hop passed through the earlier ones. If any hop below shows lower loss, the loss above it is not affecting traffic. Real loss starts at some hop and persists through every hop after it, including the destination. The final row is the meaningful figure for end-to-end loss.

For the same reason, an intermediate hop can report higher latency than the destination beyond it. Generating a TTL-exceeded reply is low-priority work, so the measured time includes that delay rather than reflecting the real forwarding path. Again, the final row is the meaningful figure.

Hops shown as ??? are routers that never answered, usually because they are configured not to send ICMP TTL-exceeded messages at all. Hop 1 is the exception: its address is read from the routing table, so a silent gateway is still shown by address and labelled (gateway).

In TCP mode the round-trip times for intermediate hops are coarse. They are derived from when the captured reply is delivered by the packet driver, which batches deliveries, so the figures can be quantised to a much larger interval than the true latency. Treat TCP mode as authoritative for the path and for loss, and use ICMP mode when latency measurements matter.

The table redraws in place using ANSI cursor movement, which works in Windows Terminal, conhost, and the VS Code integrated terminal. When output is redirected or piped, it falls back to printing each cycle sequentially rather than emitting escape sequences the destination cannot render.

dev:remarks.maml:para: Traces to 4.2.2.4 with the defaults: ICMP echo, up to 30 hops, a one-second cycle once the path settles, a one-second per-probe timeout, and reverse DNS enabled.
Traces using TCP connections to port 25, the equivalent of mtr -T -P 25. Use this to find which hop blocks a specific service, rather than where ICMP stops.

Traces TCP 445 with a longer per-probe timeout. Raising the timeout in TCP mode avoids SYN retransmission making an adequate TTL look like a failure, which would place the destination further out than it really is.
Traces to google.com showing IP addresses only, with no reverse-DNS lookups.

Lists the available adapters, then sends the probes from the Ethernet interface specifically. Useful on a machine with both a VPN tunnel and a physical NIC, to confirm which path a destination is actually reached over.
Probes once every five seconds instead of every second, for a long-running check that puts less traffic on the path.
